content.theory:
C++ variables declare a **type first**, just like Java:

```cpp
int age = 36;
double height = 1.65;
bool isStudent = true;
char grade = 'A';          // single quotes
std::string name = "Ada";  // from <string>
```

Common types:

| Type | Stores | Size |
|------|--------|------|
| `int` | whole numbers | 4 bytes |
| `double` | decimals | 8 bytes |
| `float` | decimals (less precise) | 4 bytes |
| `bool` | true/false | 1 byte |
| `char` | one character | 1 byte |
| `std::string` | text | — |

To use `std::string`, add `#include <string>` at the top.

Two const-like keywords:

- `const int MAX = 10;` — can't change (C-style, recommended)
- `#define MAX 10` — preprocessor macro (older style)

C++ is **strongly typed** — assigning a wrong type usually won't compile. Concatenate with `+`:

```cpp
std::string msg = "Score: " + std::to_string(score);
```

exercise.instruction: Complete the program: declare an int 'level' = 3 and a std::string 'world' = "Dungeon", then print: Hero is at level 3 in Dungeon.
exercise.expected: Hero is at level 3 in Dungeon
hints: Hint 3: std::cout << "Hero is at level " << level << " in " << world << std::endl;
